[pagebreak]

Chronography, Volume 2 By Monden Marvayn

[pagebreak]

Technology: Perhaps the most observable instances of Chronographer technology are their ships, deemed 'helicarriers' by the masses. Drawing inspiration from Merethic era mananauts, these enormous floating ships descend upon villages. I can't fully say what capabilities these ships truly possess, but the speed at which they move suggests some otherworldly engineering we can barely comprehend. While not regularly armed, in the few cases where fabricants have fought, they have favored mysterious projectile weapons, referred to in obscure dwemer texts as "harquebus" or "harquebuses". Again, little is known about these contraptions. Certain people have also noted that many events with the Chronographers happen in a non-linear fashion. Many talk of remembering events before they happen, or waking up several days ago after having fallen asleep a week from then. Observed technologies confirm that the Chronographers are capable of time-shifts and timestops, and their incredible technology may come from the fact that they are capable of traveling to the far future, gaining access to things we haven't even conceived of yet. The final piece of their creation are Imperfections, a general term used by them to refer to the strange puzzles they grant those in need. These Imperfections cannot be classified, as each one seems to function differently. One account told of how his imperfection changed into a memory speak-box, and over time taught him the ways of a different man, eventually allowing him to win over the woman of his dreams. Others have become showers of gold, a sword in the right place. Whatever their purpose, these Imperfections all have the end goal of being helpful, which leads me to my next section Purpose: We forget at times that the Chronographers are machines, though aware and intelligent. To them, purpose, not living, is what drives them. But what purpose do they have you ask? It took many years to figure out, but accounts and evidence overwhelmingly point to what I will refer to, and what has been referred to, as integrity preservation. As time-travelers, the Chronographers have knowledge of events before they happen. But rather than try to take advantage of these, they are content with a more noble goal, and try to prevent such events from NOT happening. By dispensing their gifts to strangers, they lightly nudge events, preserving what they no doubt believe is the integrity of time. For example, a gift given to a starving man may in time, feed him, and allow him to get back on his feet. In time, that man would lead armies, or change events significantly. It is hard to say what the end goals of this preservation is, but for now, those who receive a gift from the Chronographers should consider themselves lucky, for they have a part to play in a larger affair, and a destiny awaiting them.

[pagebreak]

Chronography, Volume 3 By Monden Marvayn

[pagebreak]

Origins: During the Battle of Mournhold, many of Sotha Sil's followers fell in battle against Mehrunes Dagon. Rather than let his comrades die, it is said that Sotha Sil reforged them into automatons of crystal. These twelve hundred saints, as history notes, became known as the Armour of Oscillating Quartz, the same faction that swayed the fabricants to leave Sotha Sil. It is believed that they believe that their reforging was done for a specific purpose, though one that would take years to come to fruition. No doubt this fueled their philosophies when convincing the fabricants to become the Chronographers as we know them now.

[pagebreak]

On Trademarks

[pagebreak]

Our Lord, the Clockwork King, believes in improving upon the designs fair Nirn has given him when he creates anew. Of course, since there is so much improvement to be done, it would be fairer to say that he draws inspiration from the designs of Nirn, as little of the original remains at the end of the iterative process. Witness the Trademark, one of his earliest such designs, based originally upon the Dreugh and designed to compensate for many of its flaws and shortcomings. Underwater, they are intelligent, blindingly fast, and enormously tough. However, their bizarre life-cycle forces them above-water for a year, whereupon they shed their octopoid lower bodies as well as much of their intelligence, becoming little better than beasts. The Trademark, at a glance, is much like a Dreugh, but with the imperfections stripped away. Lord Sotha Sil saw merit in the ability to travel between sea and land, but effected this transformation far less painfully than requiring the poor creature eat its own appendages, nor did he take their minds away in the process. A creation of war, Lord Sotha Sil spent much time devoted to the best way that the Trademark may do battle, and reached the conclusion that it had no ranged capabilities. To rectify this, it is armed with a powerful electric arc that was most decisive in fighting the Dwemeri automata. The claw was also improved somewhat, but as the Dreugh claw is already a fearsome weapon, our Lord did not devote much time to it, nor to their hide, apart from making it rust-proof. At the end of the creation cycle, he also saw fit to enable their eyes to illuminate - more for his benefit than theirs, I understand. They did not need the light to see in the crushing depths of the ocean, after all, but it evidently aided his work considerably. And then there was a brief period where he became fond of something he referred to rather cryptically as "kaijiu", so he revisited the Trademark and made them all about forty feet long. The Trademark provides a wonderfully illustrative insight into the Clockwork King's psychology, I feel.

[pagebreak]

On Sybandis

[pagebreak]

As is known, the Aurbis is a wheel with Mundus as its hub, the Earthbones alone stabilizing it and the myriad waters of Oblivion representing the gaps between the spokes. However, what is not known is that the Aedra constructed a world before Mundus to test the wisdom of Magnus's schema. To call Sybandis a world is not entirely accurate, though, as it lacks that divine spark that imbued our Mundus. It is a model for what was to come. I traveled there, once, and can say with certainty that there are few places in all the worlds so inimical to life. For you see, Sybandis lacks Divine law - it has no Earthbones. It is, after all, only a model. A precursor. It was built to test the very idea of building, and no more. It is essentially a free-floating chunk of matter in the vast, blinding expanse of Aetherius. As a consequence, Sybandis is a static world. Time does not pass, nothing grows upon the barren soil, no currents move about deep in its oceans. In that regard, it is a failure. It succeeded, however, in persuading Magnus to adopt Lorkhan's revisions to his blueprint even against his better judgement, as the world the Aedra had first created was so lacking. However, there are no divine revelations to be found there. It would only interest a particular sort of scholar interested in the construction of artificial worlds and would see the result of such an endeavor firsthand.

[pagebreak]

Journeys through Sybandis, the Nirn That Never Was, as related by Imperial Mage Cocius Ratori

[pagebreak]

My father used to work as a shipwright for the Imperial Navy. It was his pride and joy, the latent engineer in him cherished every draft and every hammer swing, and each enormous galleon he built held his love within. When support for the Navy was cut off, so were my father's projects. There wasn't enough manpower to disable the things, so they just dragged them to a nearby shore and left them there. My father still walked among those ships some nights, chasing off vandals and crabs. He'd bring me along, showing off the things he'd built. For a young boy, it was an unnerving experience. Here were these massive warships, hundreds of feet of wood and gold and magic, never to be finished, a loveletter of craftsmenship not fully penned. The ships always felt just on the brink of something, not dead, but never alive. I always felt like I was being watched by something unformed. My father must have felt it too, and though he delighted in being guardian of his fleet, there were some nights when he'd sit by a window, and look out over the Anvil bay at the ships. He called them "stillborn", and only now do I fully understand. For now, I walk through a world unfinished, where color, sound, and motion are unwritten. This is the World That Never Was, this was the practice session, the prototype plane that the gods built just to see if it would work. This is Sybandis, the Stillborn Nirn. It is simple to understand, as I said, it's simply a proof of concept, a testbed of cosmic idea. But no spirits died to make this world real, there is no law, no physics. It is a world half-built, even now as I speak I weave through unmoving flocks of skinless birds, scale mountains that have fallen away to reveal the gearwork underneath, and weave between giant scaffolding caught in mid-fall. I am the only thing real here, and even that might falter. It is no wonder that the Psjiics have put mystic locks on the entire realm, and even the Daedra avoid this silent place, fearful that its Wheels might hunger, and new Earth Bones might be formed. To even navigate this not-world, to even breathe, I must carry pieces of existence with me. A rock from a Tamriel shore, a bottle of water, not for drinking. All to remind this world that I exist. But one must take care, a foot out of place, a stumble, and you may turn an errant wheel or push down a rogue piston. And when you do, the world chugs to life, your motion and heat giving it a brief stop. The birds fly, the scaffold falls, and for a moment, you might believe this world could live, should live. But it won't. You can't turn these wheels without great cost. You see there is no sun in Sybandis, the only thing that hangs in its bleak sky is the Eye. A great lidless pupil that sits there, unmoving, unblinking, the only proof that Sybandis has a spirit. But it flares to life, even for a brief instant, the eye, that horrible eye, slowly moves it gaze towards you. I don't know want to know what happens if that eye finishes its search. I have theories, but none of which I want to test. Sybandis is a unliving world, and it is best if it stays that way.
